extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, logic, and the philosophy of science (readers studying induction and causation)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and analysis of the Law of Universal Causation and the concept of cause for the purposes of inductive logic; clarifies what counts as a cause, how causes relate to conditions, and how causation grounds inductive inference. Useful for understanding foundations and correct usage of causal claims in scientific reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Universal Causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth that every fact which has a beginning has a cause; the recognition that invariability of succession is found by observation to obtain between every fact in nature and some other fact which has preceded it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the fundamental, co-extensive law of succession on which inductive logic can be founded: if every event with a beginning has some antecedent(s) invariably connected with it, then there is a law to be found and induction can be reduced to rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause defined as the antecedent which it invariably follows (not merely has followed)
rubrics_metrics.description: When speaking of 'the cause' of a phenomenon, use the antecedent which the consequent invariably follows, in the sense that, given the present constitution of things, the antecedent will always be followed by the consequent—not merely that it has always been followed in past experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition excludes mistaken symmetric causal claims (e.g., night causing day) and requires belief that the regularity will continue under current conditions; thus causal claims carry an expectation of continued invariability, not mere historical sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes must be empirical/phenomenal (physical causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purposes of inductive logic, 'cause' denotes a phenomenon (a physical antecedent), not an ontological or metaphysical 'efficient' cause beyond experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry confines itself to causes knowable from experience; no necessity to resolve metaphysical debates about 'ultimate' causes—the practical notion of cause is the invariant antecedent(s) observable in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex causation: cause is the concurrence (sum) of several antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: An invariable sequence usually subsists between a consequent and the sum of several antecedents; the true 'cause' is the whole set of conditions (positive and negative) whose concurrence is requisite to produce the consequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common practice singles out one antecedent as 'the cause' and treats others as 'conditions' for convenience, but for scientific accuracy all relevant antecedent conditions should be acknowledged (examples: eating a dish + constitution + atmosphere → death).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximate event vs antecedent states (distinction in practice, not in principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a tendency to associate causation with the proximate antecedent event rather than with antecedent states that may have existed indefinitely; both events and enduring states are legitimate conditions of a phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical fictions (e.g., calling a long-standing state a 'force' renewed at each instant) are sometimes used to make enduring conditions appear as proximate events; analysts should recognize this tendency and treat enduring conditions as genuine antecedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes include positive and negative conditions; negatives summarized as absence of counteracting causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophically the cause of a phenomenon is the sum total of positive and negative conditions taken together; negative conditions are generally the absence of preventing or counteracting causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because explicit enumeration of all negative conditions is often prolix, it's acceptable to subsume them under 'absence of counteracting causes' while remembering that counteraction is itself a causal interaction and may be handled as positive causes in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent vs patient distinction is largely verbal
rubrics_metrics.description: The common distinction between an agent (that which acts) and a patient (that which is acted upon) is not fundamental: the so-called patient often contributes actively and can be regarded as an agent; all positive conditions are alike agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating the patient as merely passive in causal accounts; examples show stone and earth equally active in gravitational interaction, and organismal properties often co-determine effects attributed to external agents (e.g., poison + vital constitution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness requirement in stating a cause (enumeration of all conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of the cause is incomplete unless it introduces all the relevant conditions; however, in practice some conditions may be omitted if they are understood or irrelevant to the present purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: saying 'foot slipped' as cause of death omits 'weight' but is acceptable for the purpose of the account; legal or moral discourse may single out particular conditions (e.g., chairman's casting vote) for emphasis without denying the role of others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation can produce capacities or states of preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some causes have as their effect not an immediate phenomenon but the conferral of a property or capacity on an object (e.g., gunpowder prepared to explode; painting confers whiteness), which later serves as a condition for another effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such produced properties as legitimate elements of causal chains: they are 'conditions of conditions' whose production may be temporally remote from the later consequent, yet the eventual explosion (or sensory effect) still has all its immediate conditions present when it occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous universality needed for an inductive foundation; laws of number/space vs laws of succession
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of number and space exhibit rigorous universality (never defeated) but are laws of simultaneity; what is needed to found induction is a law of succession that is equally indefeasible—Law of Causation serves as that co-extensive law of succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometrical and numerical laws cannot by themselves yield laws of succession; combining them with established laws of succession can derive further succession-laws, but the foundational role requires a law applicable to successive phenomena and robust against exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and mutual testing among inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductions that can be connected by ratiocination are confirmatory of one another; conversely, inductions that imply incompatible consequences become mutual tests—showing that one must be revised or more guardedly expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger inductions can assimilate weaker ones (strengthening certainty); conflicting popular inductions (e.g., astrology) are supplanted when inconsistent with more secure scientific inductions about underlying causes.
